extracted.intended_audience: researchers, clinicians, and educators interested in child development and humor
extracted.subtask_description: A bibliographic review outlining the phylogeny and ontogenetic progression of humor and laughter from primates and infants through childhood, describing stages, triggers, cognitive/biological correlates, social dynamics, and practical implications for promoting healthy humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients/characteristics of children's humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Ingredients like incongruity, being out of place, a surprise, the unexpected, an inversion, reversals, and establishment of one's superiority through a grin, chuckle, pranks, or jokes at the expense of other people are all characteristics of their humor (Pien & Rothbart, 1976; Sinnott & Ross, 1976).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical humor examples: pratfalls, falling, clowning, foolery, being hit on the head, trickery, punning, riddles, caricature, nonsense, limericks, grotesque, exaggerations (long noses, wild hair, elongated or collapsed bodies). Use of surprise, anticlimax, inversion, and superiority are key mechanisms. These elements indicate what will likely produce laughter at different ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor styles in children (adaptive vs maladaptive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor styles in children can be adaptive (affiliative and self-enhancing) or maladaptive (aggressive and self-defeating). Self-enhancing humor benefits the self and self-defeating humor evolves later in children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a child's humor promotes social bonding and coping (affiliative/self-enhancing) or harms self/others (aggressive/self-defeating). Longitudinal associations with psychosocial adjustment and victimization (e.g., self-defeating linked to higher victimization) should be considered when classifying style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-based developmental trajectory of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor development occurs in stages aligned with cognitive development (McGhee and Piaget-related accounts): (McGhee) four stages — incongruous actions towards objects, incongruous labeling of objects and events, conceptual incongruity, humor in multiple meanings; (paper) also describes stages from sensorimotor pre-humor through preschool and early school years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map observed behaviors to stages and ages: sensorimotor pre-humor (wriggles, tickling, peek-a-boo), Stage 1 (laughter directed at attachment figures via games), Stage 2 (symbolic actions become humorous), Stage 3 (non-verbal humor: treating object as different object), Stage 4 (preschool word play, silly words), Stage 5 (≈5–7 yrs: multiple meanings, riddles/jokes). Use age gradients to interpret humor competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infant humor preconditions and early indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Infant humor emerges when infants share experiences or react to another person (shared laughter/joint attention); infant humor explained by the theory of empowerment (violating caregiver expectations) and the theory of the absurd (violations of existing schemata). First laughter emerges by 4–5 months; imagination begins ~12–18 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for shared attention, social smiling, eye contact, and reactions to peek-a-boo or surprise games. Distinguish fear reactions from safe laughter; infant humor often precedes production and is more perception/appreciation-based initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toddler humor features and emergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Toddler humor (~15–30 months onward) is object-based and includes intentional mislabeling, symbolic play, hide-and-seek, tickling, funny faces, bodily humor, funny voices, taboo/toilet humor, and misuse of objects (e.g., bowl as cap). Verbal humor emerges as intentional mislabeling and symbolic play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret mislabels as intentional jokes (not mistakes). Monitor transition from physical to verbal humor; comprehension depends on cognitive level (e.g., Piagetian tasks). Be aware of aggressive physical humor (spitting, pushing) and its socialization implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: School-age humor characteristics and social uses
rubrics_metrics.description: By early school years (4–8 yrs) children begin joke openers, memorized jokes (6–8 yrs), and by 10–14 yrs higher comprehension/production. By 10–11 yrs children understand hyperbole and exaggerated irony; affiliative styles dominate 9–11 yrs; social status correlates with laughter frequency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humor in context of social goals (attention, bonding) and academic/giftedness correlates (higher intelligence linked to greater humor). Note class-clown behavior may signal giftedness or anxiety. Use self- and peer-reports and longitudinal measures to assess stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive prerequisites for humor appreciation and production
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor in children requires imagination, perspective-taking, and language; pretense is understood from age two, various degrees of metaphor from age three, and irony from ages four to ten. Theory of mind, abstraction, and belief-based language exposure support development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess child's language/vocabulary, memory, problem-solving, and exposure to abstract family conversations or humorous books. Giftedness (vocabulary, memory, quick learning) predicts greater humor capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social facilitation and imitation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Children laugh more in social contexts: preschoolers show laughter and emotional sharing three times more with peers than adults; imitation increases laughter (e.g., laughing model vs alone increases response). Social facilitation accounts for imitative giggles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring laugh frequency, include social context (alone vs peers/adults). Experimental designs should control for models and group presence; expect higher laughter rates in peer groups and with laughing models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological and neural correlates of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor has biological bases: increased secretory immunoglobulin-A (SIgA) after humorous stimuli; neural activation differences observed in children (6–8 yrs) via fNIRS and neuroimaging with sex differences reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing physiological effects of humor consider immunological markers (SIgA) and neuroimaging (fNIRS). Interpret sex differences cautiously and in relation to temperament and age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender differences in humor development
rubrics_metrics.description: From about 6–8 years boys score higher than girls in initiation, processing, appreciation, frequency of laughter, clowning, and hostile humor; interpersonal humor perception and social distance vary by same- vs opposite-gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for gender when comparing humor initiation, style, and frequency. Consider cultural/contextual moderators; use gender-stratified analyses where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four pre-conditions/evolutionary markers of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Four pre-conditions for humor development observed in apes and children: inappropriate action, incongruous labels, incongruous features, and multiple word meanings—suggesting evolutionary continuity in humor-related behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-species comparisons cautiously to infer early preconditions; analogous play and vocalizations in non-human animals (apes, parrots, dolphins, elephants, rats, dogs) can inform hypotheses about origins of human humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and methodological indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies cited use observational recordings (laughing-crying recordings), experimental manipulations (video clips, laughing vs non-laughing models), self- and peer-reports, case studies, longitudinal studies, neuroimaging (fNIRS), and immunological measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select methods appropriate to age and research question: observational coding for infants/toddlers, self/peer reports for school-age, physiological/neural measures for mechanistic questions, and longitudinal designs to assess stability over years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor's social and developmental functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor facilitates cognitive development (imagination, perspective-taking), social bonding, sharing behaviors, coping with stress, and promotes spontaneity, optimism, and out-of-the-box thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether humor contributes to adaptive outcomes (sharing, resilience). Use measures of social competence, emotional regulation, and academic outcomes when linking humor to development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perils of negative or aggressive humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong use of humor to make negative comparisons, discriminate, humiliate, or engage in aggressive humor can result in anxiety, emotional insecurity, self- or other-directed aggression, victimization, gelotophobia/gelotophilia/katagelasticism and cyberbullying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intent, target, and social consequences of humorous acts; monitor for bullying, emotional harm, and online aggressive humor. Prevention should address social norms and empathy training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical tips for promoting healthy humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Being playful with the child, sharing stories that tickle their funny bones, allowing the child to feel superior by laughing at elders, and using humor in everyday life can be beneficial. Re-channeling aggressive tendencies into socially acceptable forms via humor is useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions should encourage affiliative/self-enhancing humor, model explicit cues to distinguish joking from pretending, use shared humorous books and play, and avoid encouraging aggressive/self-defeating humor. Monitor outcomes for social and emotional benefits.
